definition: Grammar systems theory is a field of theoretical computer science that studies systems of finite collections of formal grammars generating a formal language.
details: Each grammar works on a string, a so-called sequential form that represents an environment. Grammar systems can thus be used as a formalization of decentralized or distributed systems of agents in artificial intelligence. Let A {\displaystyle \mathbb {A} } be a simple reactive agent moving on the table and trying not to fall down from the table with two reactions, t for turning and ƒ for moving forward. The set of possible behaviors of A {\displaystyle \mathbb {A} } can then be described as formal language L A = { ( f m t n f r ) + : 1 ≤ m ≤ k ; 1 ≤ n ≤ ℓ ; 1 ≤ r ≤ k } , {\displaystyle \mathbb {L_{A}} =\{(f^{m}t^{n}f^{r})^{+}:1\leq m\leq k;1\leq n\leq \ell ;1\leq r\leq k\},} where ƒ can be done maximally k times and t can be done maximally ℓ times considering the dimensions of the table. Let G A {\displaystyle \mathbb {G_{A}} } be a formal grammar which generates language L A {\displaystyle \mathbb {L_{A}} } . The behavior of A {\displaystyle \mathbb {A} } is then described by this grammar. Suppose the A {\displaystyle \mathbb {A} } has a subsumption architecture; each component of this architecture can be then represented as a formal grammar, too, and the final behavior of the agent is then described by this system of grammars. The schema on the right describes such a system of grammars which shares a common string representing an environment. The shared sequential form is sequentially rewritten by each grammar, which can represent either a component or generally an agent. If grammars communicate together and work on a shared sequential form, it is called a Cooperating Distributed (DC) grammar system. Shared sequential form is a similar concept to the blackboard approach in AI, which is inspired by an idea of experts solving some problem together while they share their proposals and ideas on a shared blackboard. Each grammar in a grammar system can also work on its own string and communicate with other grammars in a system by sending their sequential forms on request. Such a grammar system is then called a Parallel Communicating (PC) grammar system. PC and DC are inspired by distributed AI. If there is no communication between grammars, the system is close to the decentralized approaches in AI. These kinds of grammar systems are sometimes called colonies or Eco-Grammar systems, depending (besides others) on whether the environment is changing on its own (Eco-Grammar system) or not (colonies).

explainer.lead: Grammar systems theory uses several formal grammars working together to generate a language, offering a way to describe distributed agents and their behavior. Its different communication patterns mirror shared blackboards, message passing, and decentralized systems in AI.

tiers.eli5: Imagine several writers taking turns adding to the same story, each following its own rules. The finished stories show what the whole group can do. Grammar systems theory uses this idea to describe agents: sometimes they share one workspace, sometimes they send their work to each other, and sometimes they work separately.
tiers.practitioner: It is used as a formal modelling framework rather than a software library: represent agents or components as grammars, then specify whether they rewrite a shared sequential form, exchange their own forms, or operate independently. A central pitfall is choosing the wrong communication model, since DC, PC, colonies, and Eco-Grammar systems encode different coordination assumptions. The generated language describes possible behavior, not an implementation or a learning procedure.
tiers.paperLevel: A grammar system is a finite collection of formal grammars generating a formal language. In the reactive-agent example, L_A = {(f^m t^n f^r)^+ : 1 <= m <= k, 1 <= n <= l, 1 <= r <= k}, with f denoting forward motion and t denoting a turn. DC systems sequentially rewrite a shared sequential form; PC systems maintain separate forms communicated on request; colonies and Eco-Grammar systems lack inter-grammar communication, with the environment changing autonomously only in the latter.

explainer.example: For an agent on a table, let f mean move forward and t mean turn, with k = 2 and l = 1. The string fftf means two forward moves, one turn, and one final forward move, and it belongs to L_A = {(f^m t^n f^r)^+ : 1 <= m <= 2, 1 <= n <= 1, 1 <= r <= 2}. A grammar generating this language describes those allowed behaviors; with a subsumption architecture, separate component grammars can jointly describe the agent.

usedIn.name: Theoretical computer science
usedIn.detail: Studies finite collections of formal grammars and the formal languages they generate.

usedIn.name: Distributed artificial intelligence
usedIn.detail: Provides formal models for shared-workspace, communicating, and decentralized multi-agent systems.

usedIn.name: Reactive agent modelling
usedIn.detail: Represents an agent's possible action sequences and subsumption-architecture components as grammars.

explainer.intuition: Treat each agent or component as a grammar whose rewriting rules describe what it can do. Their coordination and their access to an environment-shaped string determine the behavior generated by the whole system.
howItWorks: Represent the environment or an agent's current work as a string called a sequential form.
Associate each agent or architectural component with a formal grammar.
Let the grammars rewrite the shared form in turn in a Cooperating Distributed system.
Alternatively, let each grammar maintain its own form and send it on request in a Parallel Communicating system.
Take the generated formal language as the description of the system's possible behavior.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects formal-language generation with models of decentralized and distributed agency. The shared sequential form also gives a formal counterpart to AI's blackboard approach, where participants contribute to a common workspace.
misconceptions: It is not about checking natural-language grammar; these formal grammars generate strings and languages.
DC and PC systems are not interchangeable: DC systems share one sequentially rewritten form, while PC systems communicate separate forms on request.
Colonies and Eco-Grammar systems both lack inter-grammar communication, but an Eco-Grammar system's environment can change on its own.
